steps: Step 1, Start in ancient Greece. The ancient games were held at Olympia, traditionally dated from 776 BCE, every four years in honour of Zeus. A truce let athletes travel safely. They were ended around 393 CE.

Step 2, Move to the revival. Pierre de Coubertin helped found the International Olympic Committee on 23 June 1894. The first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896 with roughly a dozen or more nations (sources differ). Women first competed in 1900 in Paris.

Step 3, Calculate the numbering. Paris hosted in 2024. (2024 - 1896) / 4 = 32, so it was the 33rd Olympiad counting 1896 as the first. Games were cancelled in 1916, 1940 and 1944 because of the world wars, but the count continues.

Step 4, Learn symbols and values. The five rings stand for the continents joined together, and the motto is Citius, Altius, Fortius: faster, higher, stronger. Olympic values are excellence, friendship and respect. Winter Games began at Chamonix in 1924.

Step 5, Link to society. The Paralympic Games began as an official event in Rome in 1960 and now run alongside the Olympics. Write a model answer: 'Sport can unite people across nations and promote fair play, while hosting costs and doping show the challenges.'
Step 6, Your turn: what does 'respect' mean in Olympic values? Model answer: 'It means treating opponents, officials and rules fairly, such as shaking hands after a match whether you win or lose.'

Step 1, Fitness has components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, flexibility and body composition. For a 16-year-old at 60 kg and 1.65 m, BMI is 60 / (1.65 x 1.65) = 60 / 2.7225 = 22.0. Adults use 18.5 to 24.9 as normal; teenagers are compared on age-based BMI charts.

Step 2, Set heart rate zones. Estimated maximum is 220 - 16 = 204 beats per minute. Moderate to vigorous training of 60 to 85 percent gives about 122 to 173 beats per minute. Count your pulse for 15 seconds after a run and multiply by 4.

Step 3, Apply the FITT idea. Frequency: 5 days a week. Intensity: 70 percent of maximum. Time: 30 to 45 minutes. Type: running, cycling and body-weight exercises. Health guidance for young people is about 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily; check the current figure.

Step 4, Draw a weekly plan. Mon: 30 min jog. Tue: strength circuit with squats and push-ups. Wed: rest or stretching. Thu: interval run. Fri: swim or cycle. Sat: team game. Sun: walk. Add 8 to 10 hours of sleep and regular water.

Step 5, Track progress. Week 1 test: 1.6 km run in 11 minutes and 15 push-ups. After 8 weeks, record again: 9 minutes 30 seconds and 25 push-ups. That is 1.5 minutes faster and 10 more push-ups. Write what you changed and what helped.
Step 6, Your turn: a student of age 17 wants a heart-rate range of 60 to 85 percent. Model answer: 'Maximum is 203. Range is 0.60 x 203 = 122 to 0.85 x 203 = 173 beats per minute.'

Step 1, Explain sensation and perception. Sensation is when receptors detect a stimulus, such as light on the retina, and send nerve signals. Perception is the brain organising and interpreting them. You sense patches of colour and edges; you perceive a friend's face. The same sensation can be perceived differently.

Step 2, Explain thresholds. The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus you can detect, such as a faint sound. The just noticeable difference grows with the starting size. If you notice 2 g added to 100 g (2 percent), you need about 10 g added to 500 g, since 2 percent of 500 is 10.

Step 3, Explain how we organise what we see. Figure and ground: we see a shape against a background. Grouping: close or similar items look like one set. Constancy: an opening door still looks rectangular. Depth cues include overlap and relative size, so a smaller car looks farther away.

Step 4, Explain classical learning. A bell is rung just before food. Food is the unconditioned stimulus and salivation the unconditioned response. After several pairings the bell alone causes salivation, now a conditioned response. Everyday case: feeling nervous at the sound of a dentist's drill.

Step 5, Explain operant and observational learning. Behaviour followed by a reward becomes more likely: a child gets a sticker each time she tidies and tidies more. Punishment makes a behaviour less likely. In observational learning we copy what we see others do and see rewarded.

Step 6, Your turn: a child is praised each time she reads aloud and reads more often. Which learning is this, and what is the difference between sensation and perception? Answer: operant learning by positive reinforcement; sensation detects the signal, perception interprets it.

Step 1, Describe memory as encoding (taking information in), storage (keeping it) and retrieval (getting it back). Sensory memory holds impressions for only a second or a few seconds. Short-term memory holds roughly seven items, plus or minus two, for a short time, often under half a minute without rehearsal. Long-term memory can hold a huge amount for years.

Step 2, Show chunking. The digits 9876543210 are 10 items, too many to hold. Group them as 98765 and 43210 and there are two chunks. Rehearsal and mnemonics help too. Describe forgetting: decay, interference from similar items, and failure to retrieve, as in the tip-of-the-tongue feeling.

Step 3, Describe thinking: forming concepts, reasoning and solving problems. Steps are understand, plan, try, check. A three-digit lock has 1,000 codes from 000 to 999. An algorithm tries all of them; a heuristic uses clues, like a hint that all digits are odd, which cuts the options to 125.

Step 4, Describe motivation as the force that starts and keeps behaviour going. Intrinsic motivation comes from interest in the task; extrinsic comes from rewards or fear. A needs hierarchy runs from food and safety through belonging and respect to personal growth, and lower needs usually press first.

Step 5, Describe emotion as having three parts: body changes, such as a heart rate rising from 70 to 95 beats a minute before an exam; a feeling; and expression, such as a smile or frown. Slow breathing, in for 4 seconds and out for 6, can calm the body.
Step 6, Your turn: chunk the number 4729156380 into groups that are easier to hold. Answer: 472 915 6380, three chunks instead of ten separate digits; or 47291 56380 for two chunks.

Step 1, Date the policy phases. Planning began with the first Five Year Plan in 1951, which stressed agriculture, and from 1956 the plans gave priority to public sector heavy industry. By 1991 a balance of payments crisis, with very low foreign exchange reserves, led to reforms.

Step 2, Explain the 1991 reforms. They are summarised as liberalisation (fewer licences), privatisation (smaller state role in some sectors) and globalisation (lower import duties, foreign investment). Model answer should state both gains and costs in a balanced way.

Step 3, Compute growth. If GDP rises from 1,000 to 1,060 units, growth is (1,060 - 1,000) / 1,000 x 100 = 6 percent. If population grows 1.5 percent, per capita income grows roughly 4.5 percent, which affects living standards.

Step 4, Read sector shares. Agriculture has employed a large share of workers, often near 40 to 45 percent, but produces under 20 percent of output (check the current figure), so productivity per worker is low there. This gap explains why rural incomes lag and why shifting work to industry and services is a goal.

Step 5, Measure poverty. Head count ratio = poor / population x 100. If 220 million of 1,000 million live below the poverty line, the ratio is 22 percent. Compare using HDI as well, which includes health and education, not just income.

Step 6, Your turn: assess one effect of the 1991 reforms. Model answer: 'Services and exports grew faster because of openness, but inequality between regions and sectors persisted, so growth needs jobs and skills too.'

Step 1, Explain what an attitude is: a lasting evaluation of a person, object or idea. It has three parts: affective (feelings), behavioural (actions) and cognitive (beliefs). For recycling, a student may believe it helps (cognitive), feel good about it (affective) and sort waste at home (behavioural).

Step 2, Explain attitude change. Attitudes come from family, experience and media. A message works better with a credible source, clear facts and a listener who is ready to hear it. In cognitive dissonance, a student who thinks cheating is wrong but copies once may change the belief to 'everyone does it' to reduce discomfort.

Step 3, Explain social influence. Conformity is yielding to real or imagined group pressure. In a classic line-judging experiment, when every other member gave a wrong answer, about one answer in three was also wrong. Compliance is agreeing to a request; obedience is following an order from an authority.

Step 4, Explain group processes. Groups have norms, roles and cohesiveness. Social facilitation: others watching can improve a simple task. Social loafing: effort drops in a team. In an invented rope-pull each person alone pulls 60 units, but three together pull 150 in all, so 150 / 3 = 50 each, 83 percent of the solo effort.

Step 5, Explain bystanders. The more people who see an emergency, the more each may assume someone else will help; this is diffusion of responsibility. Naming one person, 'You in the blue shirt, call an adult', breaks it. Leaders and clear roles also improve group decisions.

Step 6, Your turn: alone each person pulls 40 units; a group of 4 pulls 120 in total. Find each person's pull and the percentage drop. Answer: 120 / 4 = 30 each; 30 / 40 = 75 percent, a 25 percent drop, showing social loafing.
